questions.question: Which Roman emperor tried to make his horse a consul?

answers.text: Caligula
Nero
Commodus

questions.fun_fact: Caligula reportedly planned to appoint his beloved horse Incitatus to the consulship — historians debate whether he meant it or was mocking the Senate.

questions.question: What did ancient Romans use as mouthwash?

answers.text: Urine
Vinegar
Olive oil

questions.fun_fact: Portuguese urine was especially prized — the ammonia whitened teeth. Rome even taxed the urine trade under Emperor Vespasian.

questions.question: What unusual item did Cleopatra reportedly dissolve to win a bet with Mark Antony?

answers.text: A pearl earring
A gold coin
An emerald

questions.fun_fact: Pliny the Elder wrote that Cleopatra dissolved a priceless pearl in vinegar and drank it to win a wager over throwing the most expensive dinner ever.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek philosopher reportedly died from laughing at his own joke?

answers.text: Chrysippus
Socrates
Diogenes

questions.fun_fact: Chrysippus of Soli supposedly died laughing after watching a donkey eat his figs and joking that it needed wine to wash them down.

questions.question: What did Spartan boys have to do to graduate from their training?

answers.text: Steal food without getting caught
Memorize the Iliad
Build their own armour

questions.fun_fact: The agoge deliberately underfed boys to force them to steal. Getting caught meant a beating — not for stealing, but for being clumsy enough to be noticed.

questions.question: Why did ancient Egyptians shave off their eyebrows?

answers.text: To mourn a dead cat
To honour the pharaoh's birthday
To prepare for battle

questions.fun_fact: Herodotus reported that Egyptian families shaved their eyebrows when a household cat died, as cats were sacred to the goddess Bastet.

questions.question: What was the official cause of death listed for the Greek playwright Aeschylus?

answers.text: A tortoise dropped on his head by an eagle
Poisoned wine
Drowning in a fountain

questions.fun_fact: Ancient sources claim an eagle mistook Aeschylus's bald head for a rock and dropped a tortoise on it to crack the shell.

questions.question: What strange object did Roman soldiers receive part of their salary in?

answers.text: Salt
Olive oil
Wine

questions.fun_fact: The Latin word for salt allowance was 'salarium' — the root of the modern word 'salary'. Salt preserved food and was genuinely valuable.

questions.question: How did the Roman emperor Elagabalus reportedly kill dinner guests at a banquet?

answers.text: Suffocated them with flower petals
Released lions into the dining hall
Served poisoned wine

questions.fun_fact: The Historia Augusta describes Elagabalus dropping so many rose petals from the ceiling that guests smothered underneath them.

questions.question: What did Pythagoras famously forbid his followers from eating?

answers.text: Beans
Fish
Bread

questions.fun_fact: Pythagoreans considered beans unclean and possibly housing human souls. Legend says Pythagoras let assassins kill him rather than flee through a bean field.

questions.question: What did medieval monks use to glue manuscripts together that we'd find strange today?

answers.text: Boiled animal hides and fish bladders
Beeswax mixed with honey
Tree sap and egg yolks

questions.fun_fact: Isinglass — made from fish swim bladders — was a prized medieval adhesive and is still used today in some restoration work.

questions.question: Why did Tycho Brahe wear a metal prosthetic nose?

answers.text: He lost his real one in a duel over a math formula
A horse bit it off during an experiment
He was disfigured by smallpox as a child

questions.fun_fact: Brahe lost his nose tip in a 1566 sword duel with his cousin over who was the better mathematician. He wore a brass replacement for the rest of his life.

questions.question: What unusual profession existed in medieval England called a 'gong farmer'?

answers.text: Cleaning out cesspits and latrines
Ringing church bells through the night
Training falcons for the nobility

questions.fun_fact: Gong farmers were only allowed to work at night and lived in segregated areas — but they were paid extremely well, sometimes earning more than craftsmen.

questions.question: What strange phenomenon swept through Strasbourg in 1518?

answers.text: Hundreds of people danced uncontrollably for weeks
A plague of frogs filled the streets
Every clock in the city stopped at once

questions.fun_fact: The Dancing Plague of 1518 saw around 400 people dance non-stop. Some collapsed from exhaustion and reportedly died. The cause remains debated — ergot poisoning, mass hysteria, or both.

questions.question: What did Leonardo da Vinci write his private notebooks in to keep them secret?

answers.text: Mirror-image script
Ancient Phoenician
A cipher based on bird drawings

questions.fun_fact: Leonardo wrote right-to-left in mirror script, readable only by holding the page to a mirror. He was left-handed, which may have made it more natural too.

questions.question: What did medieval doctors prescribe to cure the Black Death?

answers.text: Sitting in a sewer to smell the bad air
Drinking pure spring water
Fasting for forty days

questions.fun_fact: Medieval medicine believed plague spread through 'miasma' or bad air, so some treatments involved overwhelming the body with even worse smells to drive out the disease.

questions.question: What did Cardinal Peter Damian condemn to Pope Alexander II in 1061?

answers.text: Playing chess
Reading Greek poetry
Eating peacock

questions.fun_fact: Damian condemned chess as a frivolous distraction unworthy of clergy. The disapproval was widely ignored, even by bishops who continued playing.

questions.question: What was unusual about how castle staircases were designed?

answers.text: They spiralled clockwise to favour right-handed defenders
Every step was a different height to confuse intruders
They were always built without handrails

questions.fun_fact: Clockwise spirals gave right-handed defenders coming down room to swing, while right-handed attackers coming up had the central pillar in their sword arm.

questions.question: What did the Catholic Church try to do to Halley's Comet in 1456?

answers.text: Excommunicate it
Bless it for safe passage
Declare it the eighth wonder

questions.fun_fact: Pope Callixtus III reportedly ordered prayers against the comet, which was blamed for plague and Ottoman victories. Modern historians dispute whether a formal excommunication occurred.

questions.question: What unusual job did the 'Groom of the Stool' have in the English royal court?

answers.text: Assisting the king on the toilet
Caring for the king's hunting dogs
Polishing the throne every morning

questions.fun_fact: Despite the task, it was a prized position — Grooms of the Stool gained immense political influence through their daily intimate access to the monarch.

questions.question: At the peak of Dutch tulip mania, what could a single rare tulip bulb be exchanged for?

answers.text: A canal-side house in Amsterdam
A small fishing fleet
A barrel of gold dust

questions.fun_fact: At the 1637 peak, a single Semper Augustus bulb traded for around 10,000 guilders — roughly the price of a fine Amsterdam house. The market collapsed within weeks.

questions.question: What was Napoleon's actual height in modern measurements?

answers.text: About 1.69 m, average for his era
Only 1.55 m, unusually short
Over 1.85 m, unusually tall

questions.fun_fact: The 'short Napoleon' myth came from confusion between French and English inches. His height of 5'2" in French units equalled about 5'7" English — perfectly normal.

questions.question: What did Isaac Newton spend more time studying than physics?

answers.text: Alchemy and Biblical prophecy
Music theory and opera
Horse breeding and stable design

questions.fun_fact: Newton wrote over a million words on alchemy and Biblical chronology. Economist John Maynard Keynes called him 'the last of the magicians' after reading the papers.

questions.question: What unusual injury did Marie Antoinette's hair famously suffer overnight?

answers.text: It supposedly turned white from stress
It caught fire from a chandelier
Rats chewed it during sleep

questions.fun_fact: The legend that her hair turned white the night before her execution is medically impossible — hair doesn't change colour that fast — but the story stuck for centuries.

questions.question: What strange product was Coca-Cola originally sold as?

answers.text: A medicinal tonic containing cocaine
A cleaning solution for brass
An aftershave for barbers

questions.fun_fact: Invented in 1886 by pharmacist John Pemberton, the original recipe contained coca leaf extract. Cocaine was removed around 1903, though the leaves are still used decocainised.

questions.question: What was unusual about how Catherine the Great of Russia actually died?

answers.text: She had a stroke on the toilet
She was crushed by a horse
She drowned in a bathtub

questions.fun_fact: Catherine died of a stroke in 1796 after collapsing in her water closet. The infamous 'horse' rumour was anti-Russian propaganda spread by her enemies in Europe.

questions.question: What did the 1814 London Beer Flood unleash on the streets?

answers.text: Around 1.5 million litres of beer
A cloud of brewery smoke that blocked the sun
Thousands of escaped brewery rats

questions.fun_fact: A ruptured vat at the Meux Brewery sent a wave of porter through the parish of St Giles. At least 8 people drowned in beer in their cellars and basements.

questions.question: What did Thomas Jefferson keep on display at the White House from Zebulon Pike's expedition?

answers.text: Two live grizzly bear cubs
A herd of buffalo
A captured British naval flag

questions.fun_fact: Pike sent the cubs as a gift in 1807. Jefferson kept them in cages on the White House lawn before shipping them to Charles Willson Peale's museum after they became unmanageable.

questions.question: What did the CIA spend years trying to do to Fidel Castro using a poisoned object?

answers.text: Make his beard fall out with thallium
Replace his cigars with chocolate
Steal his shoes for forensic study

questions.fun_fact: Operation Mongoose included a plan to dust Castro's shoes with thallium salts so his beard would fall out and humiliate him before a UN speech. It never happened.

questions.question: What unusual cargo did the Soviet space programme send to orbit in 1957?

answers.text: A stray Moscow street dog named Laika
A trained chimpanzee from Cuba
A live chicken to test reproduction

questions.fun_fact: Laika died within hours of launch from overheating — the Soviets admitted this only decades later. The mission had no plan to return her safely.

questions.question: What did the British actually use to camouflage ships in World War I?

answers.text: Painted dazzle patterns inspired by Cubism
Real tree branches glued to the hull
Sheets of polished mirror

questions.fun_fact: Dazzle camouflage didn't hide ships — it made it hard for U-boat crews to judge their speed and direction. Marine artist Norman Wilkinson designed the patterns.

questions.question: What weird item did the CIA try to weaponise in the 1960s under Project Acoustic Kitty?

answers.text: A surgically implanted cat
A trained pigeon with a tiny camera
A robotic squirrel

questions.fun_fact: The CIA spent around $20 million implanting a microphone in a cat to eavesdrop on Soviet diplomats. On its first mission, the cat was reportedly hit by a taxi.

questions.question: What did Salvador Dalí design for a famous brand in 1969 that we still see today?

answers.text: The Chupa Chups logo
The Coca-Cola contour bottle
The Michelin Man

questions.fun_fact: Dalí designed the daisy-shaped Chupa Chups logo on a napkin in a single afternoon. He insisted it go on top of the lollipop so it would always be visible.

questions.question: What strange phenomenon did the BBC report on April Fools' Day 1957?

answers.text: A Swiss spaghetti harvest from trees
A flying car prototype over London
A whale migration up the Thames

questions.fun_fact: The Panorama segment showed farmers picking spaghetti from trees. Hundreds of viewers called in asking how to grow their own — they were told to put a sprig in tomato sauce.

questions.question: What weird side project did Werner von Braun pursue alongside rocket science?

answers.text: Writing a sci-fi novel about Mars colonies
Designing miniature golf courses
Breeding ornamental koi fish

questions.fun_fact: His 1952 novel 'Das Marsprojekt' described a Mars mission in detail and named the colony's leader the 'Elon' — a Hebrew word meaning leader. Yes, really.

questions.question: What unusual deception did the Allies use in Operation Mincemeat in 1943?

answers.text: A corpse with fake invasion plans
Inflatable rubber tanks in Kent
Radio broadcasts in fake German

questions.fun_fact: British intelligence dressed a homeless man's corpse as a Royal Marines officer and floated it off Spain with documents suggesting an invasion of Greece, not Sicily. The Germans believed it.

questions.question: What did the United States seriously consider doing to the Moon in 1958?

answers.text: Detonating a nuclear bomb on its surface
Painting a giant US flag visible from Earth
Carving Mount Rushmore into a crater

questions.fun_fact: Project A119 planned a visible nuclear flash on the Moon as a Cold War show of force. Carl Sagan worked on it as a young scientist. The project was scrapped over public backlash fears.

questions.question: How did Australia's 1932 Emu War end?

answers.text: Australia lost to the birds
A peace treaty was signed with emu advocates
All the emus were captured and zoo-bound

questions.fun_fact: The Australian military fired thousands of rounds at emus damaging crops but managed only a few hundred kills. The emus scattered into small groups and outran the soldiers. The military withdrew.

questions.question: What was the duration of the shortest war in history, between Britain and Zanzibar in 1896?

answers.text: Around 38 minutes
About 6 hours
Just under 3 days

questions.fun_fact: The Anglo-Zanzibar War ended after British warships shelled the palace. Estimates range from 38 to 45 minutes — fast enough that nobody quite agrees on the exact number.

questions.question: What ridiculous event caused the 1925-1926 War of the Stray Dog between Greece and Bulgaria?

answers.text: A soldier chased his dog across the border
Bulgaria refused to return a royal pet
A pack of dogs ate a diplomat's lunch

questions.fun_fact: A Greek soldier crossed into Bulgaria chasing his dog and was shot. Greece invaded. The League of Nations intervened and forced a withdrawal within days.

questions.question: What unlikely weapon did the US develop in World War II called the Bat Bomb?

answers.text: Bats carrying tiny incendiary devices
Baseball-bat-shaped depth charges
Sonar mimicking actual bat calls

questions.fun_fact: Thousands of Mexican free-tailed bats were fitted with timed napalm capsules to roost in Japanese buildings before igniting. A test accidentally burned down a US Army airfield.

questions.question: What unusual plan did the British MI5 propose to assassinate Hitler that was rejected?

answers.text: Lacing his tea with female hormones
Hiding a bomb inside an Oscar statue
Replacing his moustache wax with explosive paste

questions.fun_fact: Operation Foxley considered injecting oestrogen into Hitler's food to make him less aggressive and bald. Planners ultimately worried that a martyred Hitler would rally Germany.

questions.question: What strange object caused the Pig War of 1859 between Britain and the US?

answers.text: A single pig eating potatoes
A stolen sow worth a fortune
A pig parade gone wrong

questions.fun_fact: An American farmer shot a British-owned pig on San Juan Island. Both sides sent troops. Despite weeks of standoff, the only casualty was the pig itself.

questions.question: What was unusual about the soldiers who fought the Battle of Castle Itter in May 1945?

answers.text: Americans and Germans fought side by side
It was fought entirely in snowshoes
Both sides used wooden rifles

questions.fun_fact: US troops and Wehrmacht defectors jointly defended French VIP prisoners against the SS. It's the only known WWII battle where Americans and Germans fought together.

questions.question: What odd outcome did the Football War of 1969 between El Salvador and Honduras have?

answers.text: It lasted only 100 hours
It was decided by a penalty shootout
Both sides claimed FIFA membership in victory

questions.fun_fact: Tensions over World Cup qualifiers ignited deeper disputes over land and migration. The fighting lasted four days, killed around 3,000, and disrupted the region for years.

questions.question: What did Soviet tank crews do to keep their engines running through the winter of 1941-42?

answers.text: Sprayed perfume on tanks to mask diesel
Wrapped engines in dog fur from sled teams
Mixed kerosene into the engine oil

questions.fun_fact: Soviet crews thinned their oil with kerosene to keep it flowing at minus 40°C. It worked — German engines just froze solid, immobilising whole panzer divisions.

questions.question: What ridiculous reason did Paraguay give for declaring war on the Allies in February 1945?

answers.text: To qualify for UN founding membership
To honour an old colonial treaty
To recover a stolen presidential carriage

questions.fun_fact: Several Latin American countries declared war on Germany weeks before the war ended specifically to be invited to the San Francisco UN founding conference. Paraguay sent no troops.

questions.question: What did ancient Romans use to whiten their togas?

answers.text: Stale urine collected from public latrines
A paste of crushed seashells
Sap from cedar trees

questions.fun_fact: Fullers used ammonia from aged urine to bleach wool. Pots stood on Roman street corners for citizens to contribute — and the cloth-cleaners paid the city for the privilege.

questions.question: What did the ancient Aztecs use cocoa beans for besides drinking?

answers.text: As currency to buy goods
As ammunition in slingshots
As decorative beads in jewellery

questions.fun_fact: A turkey could cost around 100 cocoa beans and a fresh avocado just three. Counterfeit beans made from clay were a known problem in Aztec markets.

questions.question: What surprising material were the first toothbrushes with bristles made from?

answers.text: Hog hair set in bamboo or bone
Braided silk threads dipped in wax
Fine copper wire wrapped in linen

questions.fun_fact: Bristle toothbrushes appeared in Tang-era China using stiff hairs from the necks of cold-climate pigs. European travellers later copied the design and substituted horsehair.

questions.question: What unusual currency did the people of Yap Island use for centuries?

answers.text: Giant stone wheels over three metres wide
Polished whale teeth on cords
Strings of dried coconut shells

questions.fun_fact: Some Rai stones were too heavy to move, so ownership simply transferred verbally — everyone on the island just remembered who owned which stone. One famous stone sat at the bottom of the sea and still counted as wealth.

questions.question: What strange material did ancient Egyptians use to preserve mummies' organs?

answers.text: Natron salt scooped from desert lakes
Crushed lapis lazuli paste
Crocodile fat boiled with myrrh

questions.fun_fact: Natron is a naturally occurring mix of sodium carbonate and bicarbonate. Embalmers packed bodies in it for around 40 days to draw out all moisture before wrapping.

questions.question: What did Vikings actually wear on their heads in battle?

answers.text: Simple iron or leather caps with no horns
Bronze helmets shaped like animal skulls
Hoods of seal skin lined with fur

questions.fun_fact: The horned-helmet image came from 19th-century opera costumes for Wagner's Ring cycle. Archaeology has produced only two near-complete Viking helmets — the Gjermundbu from Norway and the Yarm helmet from Yorkshire — and neither has horns.

questions.question: What did medieval European peasants drink instead of water at most meals?

answers.text: Weak ale called small beer
Boiled goat's milk with herbs
Tea brewed from hedgerow leaves

questions.fun_fact: Small beer was so dilute that even children drank it. The brewing process killed waterborne pathogens, making it safer than river water in towns.

questions.question: What odd thing did the city of Paris ban in 1530 for safety reasons?

answers.text: Throwing chamber pot contents out of windows
Wearing wooden clogs after dark
Riding horses across the Pont Neuf

questions.fun_fact: Tossers were supposed to shout 'gardez l'eau' — 'watch out for the water' — before emptying pots. The phrase is one source theory for the English word 'loo'.

questions.question: What did the Library of Alexandria reportedly do to every ship that docked in the harbour?

answers.text: Confiscated and copied any books on board
Demanded a written poem as a docking fee
Searched the crew for hidden maps

questions.fun_fact: Ptolemaic officials kept the originals and returned the copies, building one of antiquity's largest collections. The owners were rarely amused but had little choice.

questions.question: What did Mongol warriors carry under their saddles on long campaigns?

answers.text: Raw meat that tenderised as they rode
Spare bowstrings wrapped in silk
Sacks of fermented millet for currency

questions.fun_fact: The friction and sweat softened tough cuts during the day. Whether this is the true origin of steak tartare is debated, but the practice itself was widely recorded by travellers.

questions.question: What unusual perk did Roman gladiators' sweat reportedly become?

answers.text: A sought-after ingredient in face creams
An offering burned at temple altars
A flavouring sprinkled on imperial bread

questions.fun_fact: Vendors scraped the mix of sweat, oil and arena dust from a gladiator's skin with a strigil and bottled it as a beauty product. Wealthy Roman women paid handsomely.

questions.question: What did sailors traditionally drink instead of water on long Royal Navy voyages?

answers.text: A daily ration of rum mixed with water
Vinegar diluted with lemon juice
Strong tea boiled with ginger

questions.fun_fact: The diluted rum was called 'grog' after Admiral Edward Vernon's nickname 'Old Grog'. The daily ration was finally abolished by the Royal Navy in 1970.

questions.question: What did the city of Edinburgh's residents shout out their windows before throwing waste?

answers.text: 'Gardyloo!'
'Heads below!'
'Mind the burn!'

questions.fun_fact: The cry was a corruption of the French 'gardez l'eau'. Tenement dwellers gave only a moment's warning before chamber pots emptied into the High Street.

questions.question: What surprising material were ancient Roman concrete sea walls made stronger by?

answers.text: Volcanic ash that reacted with seawater
Crushed seashells from oyster farms
Iron filings from forge workshops

questions.fun_fact: Pozzolana ash from around Vesuvius reacts with calcium and seawater to form crystals that actually grow over centuries — which is why Roman harbour ruins are still standing.

questions.question: What did medieval European kings often appoint a special person to do at meals?

answers.text: Taste every dish before they ate
Recite a poem between courses
Polish each piece of cutlery in view

questions.fun_fact: Food tasters checked for poison and worked for surprisingly long careers — many monarchs preferred trusting familiar people over rotating in fresh ones.

questions.question: What odd structure did Persian king Xerxes order built across the Hellespont in 480 BC?

answers.text: A floating bridge of lashed-together ships
A stone causeway sunk by slaves
A chain of rafts pulled by elephants

questions.fun_fact: When a storm destroyed the first bridge, Xerxes ordered the sea itself whipped 300 times as punishment. The engineers were beheaded; the rebuilt bridge held.

questions.question: What did Inca messengers called chasquis use to carry information across the empire?

answers.text: Knotted cords called quipus
Painted clay tablets baked in the sun
Carved wooden sticks dyed by region

questions.fun_fact: A relay of trained runners could move quipus from Cusco to Quito — over 2,000 km — in about a week. The knot patterns encoded numbers and likely narrative content.

questions.question: What did Henry VIII famously do with his lute strings between meals?

answers.text: Played and composed his own music
Wore them as decorative wristbands
Sold them to court ladies as charms

questions.fun_fact: Henry was a competent musician and wrote dozens of pieces. The song 'Greensleeves' has long been credited to him, though musicologists now consider that attribution dubious.

questions.question: What was the surprising main fuel of medieval European castles' kitchens?

answers.text: Wood, requiring vast forest reserves
Peat dug from monastery bogs
Whale oil shipped from the north

questions.fun_fact: A large household could burn through hundreds of cartloads of wood a year. Some kings kept entire forests reserved purely to feed the royal kitchens and hearths.

questions.question: What did the residents of Pompeii leave behind that surprised 18th-century excavators?

answers.text: Painted advertisements and rude graffiti
Detailed star charts on every wall
Wooden boards listing daily lottery winners

questions.fun_fact: Walls feature election posters, brothel adverts, and insults like 'Successus was here'. The scratched messages are one of antiquity's richest windows into ordinary speech.

questions.question: What did Roman Emperor Claudius famously have a stutter and limp from?

answers.text: A likely childhood illness
A javelin wound from a training accident
Years of being kicked by palace horses

questions.fun_fact: Claudius's family hid him away because they thought him an embarrassment. The disregard probably saved his life during Caligula's purges — and he ended up emperor.

questions.question: What surprising profession did the Inca empire formally employ called a 'quipucamayoc'?

answers.text: Reader of knotted-cord records
Counter of llamas at mountain passes
Painter of temple sun symbols

questions.fun_fact: Quipucamayocs were trusted accountants and historians whose knot-reading skill took years to master. After the Spanish conquest, surviving quipucamayocs were often consulted as living archives.

questions.question: What did Renaissance Florence's wealthy citizens do with their pet falcons?

answers.text: Listed them in their wills as valuable estate
Trained them to deliver perfumed letters
Released them at funerals as a status display

questions.fun_fact: A trained hunting falcon could be more valuable than a horse. Owners listed individual birds by name in wills and inventories alongside silverware and jewellery.

questions.question: What unusual feature did Roman emperor Trajan's column in Rome originally have?

answers.text: A spiral interior staircase to the top
Hollow chambers used as imperial wine cellars
Bronze plates that rang in the wind

questions.fun_fact: Almost 200 narrow steps spiral up inside the column. Lit by small slits, it ends at a platform where Trajan's statue once stood — replaced in 1588 by a statue of St Peter.

questions.question: What did the inhabitants of medieval Iceland use instead of stone for major buildings?

answers.text: Stacked turf and driftwood
Whalebone frames thatched with kelp
Volcanic glass slabs cut by hand

questions.fun_fact: Iceland had almost no native trees and limited workable stone. Turf walls metres thick kept houses warm through winters — and required rebuilding every few decades.

questions.question: What did King Charles II of England keep at his palace alongside his courtiers?

answers.text: A herd of pet spaniels with run of the rooms
A collection of trained pickpockets
A working blacksmith's forge

questions.fun_fact: The dogs slept in the king's bed and followed him into council meetings. The breed we now call the King Charles Spaniel keeps his name and the same general look.

questions.question: What did the ancient Olympics require all male athletes to do during competition?

answers.text: Compete completely naked
Speak only in rhymed couplets
Wear a wreath made of laurel and bronze

questions.fun_fact: The Greek word 'gymnos' means naked — the root of 'gymnasium'. One reason married women were barred as spectators on pain of death, though unmarried girls could watch.

questions.question: What did the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan have that astonished the arriving Spanish in 1519?

answers.text: Streets so clean they were swept daily
A canal system longer than all of Venice combined
Public stadiums seating 100,000 people

questions.fun_fact: Hundreds of municipal workers swept the streets and emptied public latrines into boats for night-soil collection. Spanish chroniclers compared the city favourably to anywhere in Europe.

questions.question: What did medieval lords stockpile as a strategic resource in their cellars?

answers.text: Barrels of salted herring
Bricks of pressed tea leaves
Boxes of dried saffron threads

questions.fun_fact: Salted herring kept for months and powered fasting-day meals across Catholic Europe. The Hanseatic League grew rich largely on the Baltic herring trade.

questions.question: What strange device did Greek inventor Heron of Alexandria reportedly build in the first century?

answers.text: A working steam-powered toy
A self-loading crossbow
A mechanical writing arm

questions.fun_fact: His aeolipile was a hollow sphere that spun when heated water inside turned to jetting steam. Treated as a curiosity, it never developed into anything practical for almost 1,700 years.

questions.question: What surprising service did medieval European monasteries widely provide travellers?

answers.text: Free overnight lodging and meals
Currency exchange between local mints
Trained dogs to guide them to the next town

questions.fun_fact: The Rule of St Benedict obliged monasteries to receive guests 'as Christ'. The hostel tradition created a continent-wide network long before formal inns existed.

questions.question: What did the residents of medieval London sometimes do when the Thames froze solid?

answers.text: Held full markets and bonfires on the ice
Carved temporary chapels into the surface
Raced wooden sleds for cash prizes

questions.fun_fact: The 'Frost Fairs' featured printing presses, fairground rides and roasted ox. The last big one was 1814 — after that, a new London Bridge let water flow faster and the Thames stopped freezing solid.

questions.question: What odd diplomatic gift did Sultan Hārūn al-Rashīd send Charlemagne around 802 AD?

answers.text: A live elephant called Abul-Abbas
A library of one thousand bound books
A solid silver model of Baghdad

questions.fun_fact: The elephant walked from Baghdad to Aachen via North Africa and Italy. Charlemagne paraded Abul-Abbas at court and on military expeditions until the animal died around 810.

questions.question: What did medieval European universities sometimes require students to do during exams?

answers.text: Defend their thesis aloud against any challenger for hours
Compose a sonnet in Latin while standing
Demonstrate juggling as a sign of dexterity

questions.fun_fact: The 'disputatio' could last all day. A student had to handle objections in real time from masters and any spectator — both training and ritual humiliation rolled into one.

questions.question: What did the ancient Roman aqueduct system deliver to the city beyond drinking water?

answers.text: Water for public fountains, baths and toilets
A daily ration of imported snowmelt
Heated water piped from natural hot springs

questions.fun_fact: At its peak Rome had 11 aqueducts feeding around 1,000 public fountains, hundreds of baths, and the famous Cloaca Maxima sewer — which is still functioning today as part of modern Rome's drainage.

questions.question: What unusual practice did the Hittites use in diplomacy around 1259 BC?

answers.text: Signed one of history's earliest written peace treaties
Exchanged child hostages dressed as priests
Required envoys to walk on hot coals

questions.fun_fact: The treaty of Kadesh between Hittites and Egyptians survives in cuneiform and hieroglyphic versions. A copy hangs at the UN headquarters in New York as a symbol of early diplomacy.

questions.question: What surprising material did Byzantine emperors use to seal their most important documents?

answers.text: Lead discs stamped with imperial insignia
Beeswax mixed with powdered sapphires
Resin from Lebanese cedar boiled with gold

questions.fun_fact: The 'bulla' gave us the word 'bull' as in 'papal bull'. Heavy lead seals deterred forgery and survived in archives for over a millennium.

questions.question: What did medieval guild apprentices typically receive instead of regular wages?

answers.text: Room, board, training and clothes only
A daily ration of silver coins from the guild
Free entry to all city festivals

questions.fun_fact: Apprenticeships could last seven years. Only after producing a 'masterpiece' judged by the guild could a journeyman set up his own workshop and start charging customers.

questions.question: What did ancient Chinese emperors employ a special official to taste before serving?

answers.text: Every dish and every cup of wine
Each pinch of incense burned at altars
Every brush of ink used in proclamations

questions.fun_fact: The 'taster' role existed in imperial courts from the Han dynasty onward. Silver chopsticks were also used because some poisons were believed to tarnish silver.

questions.question: What did the Romans build at Bath in England specifically for the local hot springs?

answers.text: A vast bathing complex around a temple to Sulis Minerva
A military prison with steam-heated walls
A floating market on stilts above the water

questions.fun_fact: Visitors threw curse tablets — sheets of inscribed lead — into the spring asking the goddess to punish thieves. Over 130 have been recovered, naming suspects in surprisingly petty disputes.

questions.question: What did medieval Venetian glassmakers do to keep their trade secrets safe?

answers.text: Were confined to the island of Murano under penalty of death
Worked only by candlelight with curtains drawn
Spoke a coded dialect in the workshop

questions.fun_fact: Murano artisans enjoyed high status and could marry into the nobility — but leaving Venice to set up workshops abroad was treated as treason and assassins were sent after defectors.

questions.question: What did Egyptian pharaoh Hatshepsut do that was unusual for a queen regnant?

answers.text: Wore a false ceremonial beard
Spoke only through male translators
Refused to be depicted in any artwork

questions.fun_fact: Statues show Hatshepsut with the traditional pharaonic beard and male regalia. Her stepson Thutmose III later had many of her images defaced — historians still argue whether out of malice or politics.

questions.question: What odd structure did 19th-century Londoners build largely for tourists called the Tower Subway?

answers.text: An underwater tunnel with a tiny cable-driven carriage
A floating restaurant on chains across the Thames
A glass dome housing a giant clockwork model of Big Ben

questions.fun_fact: Opened in 1870, the cable car carried a dozen people at a time. It was so slow and cramped that it became a foot tunnel within months — and still survives as a utility passage today.

questions.question: What did medieval Scandinavian sagas record being used as legal evidence?

answers.text: Sworn oaths backed by named witnesses
Patterns of bird flight observed at dawn
Dreams interpreted by appointed seers

questions.fun_fact: Icelandic 'Thing' assemblies relied on memorised oaths and witness networks. Cases could be decided by the number and standing of those willing to swear on your behalf.

questions.question: What did ancient Greek doctors often prescribe for a wide range of ailments?

answers.text: A long walk or a controlled fast
Inhaling smoke from burning olive pits
Sleeping next to a tame snake

questions.fun_fact: Hippocratic medicine emphasised diet, exercise and rest more than dramatic interventions — a philosophy that looks oddly modern compared to the bleeding-heavy medicine of much later centuries.

questions.question: What did the city of Pompeii leave behind on its sidewalks that surprised excavators?

answers.text: Embedded raised stepping stones to cross flooded streets
Coloured tiles marking the city's tax districts
Iron rings for tying up exotic pets

questions.fun_fact: Streets doubled as drains during storms. Spaced stones let pedestrians cross dry-footed, while cart wheels passed through the gaps — a clever piece of urban engineering.

questions.question: What unusual role did the cats of the Hermitage Museum in St Petersburg traditionally play?

answers.text: Official rodent control on the palace payroll
Models for in-house sculptors
Living thermometers for the gallery climate

questions.fun_fact: Empress Elizabeth brought in cats in the 1740s to handle mice. Their descendants still live in the basements with their own staff, food allowance and an annual public 'Day of the Cat'.

questions.question: What did 19th-century European doctors believe about the new habit of bicycle riding?

answers.text: It caused a dangerous condition called 'bicycle face'
It magnetised the rider's blood after long trips
It cured stammering by jolting the throat

questions.fun_fact: Newspapers warned that strained expressions and hard breathing while cycling could permanently distort the face — especially women's. The 'condition' quietly vanished as cycling became normal.

questions.question: What unusual product did the city of Cologne export to the world starting in the 1700s?

answers.text: A scented water called eau de Cologne
Hand-painted porcelain dolls in pairs
Mechanical singing birds in gilt cages

questions.fun_fact: Italian-born Giovanni Maria Farina blended a citrus scent in Cologne in 1709 and named it after his adopted city. The recipe is still made by his descendants at the original address.

questions.question: What surprising thing did Pope Gregory IX issue a papal bull against in 1233?

answers.text: Cats, especially black ones
Wearing pointed shoes in church
Eating dinner after sunset

questions.fun_fact: The bull 'Vox in Rama' linked cats with devil worship and helped fuel cat-killing campaigns. Some historians argue that fewer cats meant more rats — which mattered when the Black Death arrived a century later.

questions.question: What did the Aztecs send the Spanish in 1519 as a diplomatic offering?

answers.text: Gold ornaments, feathered cloaks and cacao
A trained jaguar in a wheeled cage
A book of constellation maps

questions.fun_fact: Moctezuma's gifts were intended to impress and perhaps to send the visitors politely away. They had the opposite effect — Cortés interpreted the gold as evidence of richer hoards inland.

questions.question: What odd habit did the Persian Achaemenid kings reportedly indulge in before big decisions?

answers.text: Debated each plan once drunk and once sober
Slept on the palace roof for three nights
Bathed in goat's milk for an entire day

questions.fun_fact: Herodotus reports the practice: any decision approved both drunk and sober was considered tested from both sides. Modern behavioural science has occasionally praised the underlying logic.

questions.question: Which everyday invention is actually older than the telephone?

answers.text: The fax machine
The television
The light bulb

questions.fun_fact: Alexander Bain patented a fax-like device in 1843, decades before Bell's 1876 telephone. It scanned a message with a pendulum and reproduced it as marks at the other end.

questions.question: Why does old glass in medieval cathedral windows look thicker at the bottom?

answers.text: It was made uneven and installed thick-side down
Glass slowly flows downward like a liquid over centuries
Centuries of rain eroded the top edge thinner

questions.fun_fact: Old crown glass was spun into uneven discs, so glaziers logically set the heavier edge at the bottom. The 'glass flows' myth is false — glass is an amorphous solid that doesn't sag at room temperature on human timescales.

questions.question: Why did Roman lead water pipes not poison everyone as badly as you'd expect?

answers.text: Hard water coated the pipes in protective mineral scale
The lead was mixed with neutralising tin
Romans boiled all water before drinking it

questions.fun_fact: Rome's water was rich in calcium carbonate, which quickly lined the pipes with limescale and sealed the lead away from the flowing water. Constantly running water also limited how long any water touched the metal.

questions.question: How did ancient ice merchants ship ice across oceans without it melting away?

answers.text: Packing it in sawdust, which insulated the blocks
Coating each block in a thick layer of beeswax
Sailing only at night and storing it below the waterline

questions.fun_fact: In the 1800s Frederic Tudor shipped New England ice as far as India. Sawdust — a waste product from sawmills — trapped air so well that losses on long voyages were surprisingly small.

questions.question: Why did sailors in the age of sail risk death without limes or lemons?

answers.text: Their bodies can't make vitamin C and collagen falls apart
Citrus was the only thing that killed seawater bacteria
The acid was needed to digest salted meat

questions.fun_fact: Scurvy is collagen failure: without vitamin C the body can't bind connective tissue, so old wounds reopen and gums rot. Humans are among the few mammals that lost the gene to synthesise their own.

questions.question: Why were medieval suits of armour surprisingly easy to move and fight in?

answers.text: The weight was spread across the whole body, not carried in the arms
The steel was hollow to save weight
Knights were winched onto horses because they couldn't walk

questions.fun_fact: A full field harness weighed about as much as a modern soldier's kit, but distributed over every limb. Fit knights could run, mount unaided and even do cartwheels — the crane-and-immobile-knight image is a Hollywood myth.

questions.question: Why did old black-and-white film actors' red lipstick photograph as black?

answers.text: Early film was blind to red light and saw it as dark
Studios used special black lipstick for contrast
Hot stage lights chemically darkened the makeup

questions.fun_fact: Orthochromatic film stock was sensitive to blue and green but barely to red, so red lips, freckles and rosy skin came out dark. Makeup artists had to paint actors in unnatural colours to look right on screen.

questions.question: Why did people in past centuries commonly sleep in two separate sessions each night?

answers.text: Without artificial light, the body naturally splits sleep in two
Laws required households to wake and check fires at midnight
Beds were too short to lie down fully in one stretch

questions.fun_fact: References to 'first sleep' and 'second sleep' fill pre-industrial writing, with a waking hour between for prayer, talk or sex. Cheap lighting compressed sleep into one block — and sleep labs have reproduced the two-phase pattern in people kept in darkness.

questions.question: Why did sourdough bread feed cities for millennia before anyone understood why it rose?

answers.text: Wild yeast and bacteria fermenting the dough release gas
Pounding the dough physically beat air bubbles into it
The heat of the oven boiled water into expanding steam pockets

questions.fun_fact: Bakers kept a 'starter' alive for generations without knowing it teemed with microbes. The yeast eat sugars and breathe out carbon dioxide that gets trapped in the gluten, puffing the loaf up.

questions.question: Why did medieval blacksmiths quench red-hot blades in liquid to harden them?

answers.text: Rapid cooling locks the steel into a hard crystal structure
The water washed impurities out of the metal
Steam pressure compressed the blade's surface

questions.fun_fact: Sudden cooling traps carbon in a brittle, hard arrangement called martensite. Smiths discovered this by trial and error centuries before metallurgy existed — and some folklore swore blades quenched in blood or urine were superior.

questions.question: Why did gold coins survive shipwrecks looking brand new while silver ones corroded?

answers.text: Gold barely reacts with anything, including seawater
Gold is heavier so it sank into protective sand faster
Gold coins were always coated in a sealing varnish

questions.fun_fact: Gold is one of the least reactive metals, so sunken hoards gleam after centuries underwater. Silver tarnishes because it reacts readily with sulphur compounds in seawater, blackening the surface.

questions.question: Why did the lime mortar in ancient buildings actually get stronger over time?

answers.text: It slowly absorbs carbon dioxide and turns back into stone
Plant roots grew through it and bound it together
Repeated rain compressed the particles tighter

questions.fun_fact: Lime mortar carbonates: it pulls CO2 from the air and reverts to calcium carbonate — essentially limestone — over years to centuries. Some Roman walls are still slowly hardening today.

questions.question: Why did ancient Egyptian wall paintings keep their bright blue colour for thousands of years?

answers.text: They used a man-made pigment that is chemically extremely stable
The tombs were filled with a preserving gas
They reapplied the paint during yearly festivals

questions.fun_fact: Egyptian blue, made by heating sand, copper and natron, is one of the oldest synthetic pigments. It's so stable it still glows under infrared light — a property modern scientists now use to detect ancient traces invisible to the eye.

questions.question: Why did a single struck match start a fire only after a chemical was added in the 1800s?

answers.text: Friction heat had to ignite a phosphorus compound on the tip
Matches needed a hidden spark of static electricity
The wood had to be soaked in alcohol first

questions.fun_fact: Early friction matches used white phosphorus, which ignites at low temperature but poisoned factory workers, rotting their jaws — 'phossy jaw'. Safer red phosphorus, split onto a separate striker strip, gave us the modern safety match.

questions.question: Why did people once put a silver coin in milk to keep it from going off?

answers.text: Silver ions actually slow bacterial growth
The coin's weight pushed cream to the bottom
Silver cooled the milk faster than the jug

questions.fun_fact: Silver has genuine antimicrobial properties — ancient peoples lined water and wine vessels with it. The effect is modest, but the underlying chemistry is real and is still used in modern wound dressings.

questions.question: Why did old lighthouses stay visible from far out at sea before electric lamps?

answers.text: Curved lenses and mirrors concentrated a flame into a beam
The flames were fed pure oxygen to burn brighter
The towers were painted with glowing phosphorescent paint

questions.fun_fact: The Fresnel lens, invented in 1822, used concentric rings of glass to bend scattered light into one powerful beam, letting a modest oil flame be seen for tens of kilometres. The same principle now sits in car headlights and traffic lights.

questions.question: Before dentists understood tooth decay, what was actually rotting people's teeth?

answers.text: Bacteria eating sugar and making acid that dissolves enamel
Teeth dissolving naturally without salt in the diet
Cold sea air cracking enamel from the inside

questions.fun_fact: Cavities are an infection: mouth bacteria ferment sugars and excrete acid that dissolves enamel. This is why tooth decay exploded only after cheap sugar arrived — skeletons from before the sugar trade have strikingly fewer cavities.

questions.question: Why did the bodies in peat bogs stay so intact that they look recently dead?

answers.text: Acidic, oxygen-free bog water tans skin and stops decay
The cold of northern bogs froze them permanently
Bog minerals turned the bodies slowly to stone

questions.fun_fact: Bog acids and a lack of oxygen halt the bacteria that cause rot, while tannins tan the skin like leather. Some bog bodies are 2,000 years old yet still show fingerprints, stubble and the contents of their last meal.

questions.question: Why did Stradivarius violins supposedly sound so good, according to one leading theory?

answers.text: A cold-climate growth spell made unusually dense, even wood
The maker sealed them with a secret gold varnish
The strings were spun from a now-extinct silkworm

questions.fun_fact: One theory ties the instruments to the 'Little Ice Age', when long cold winters produced slow, dense, uniform tree growth. The real cause is still debated, and blind tests show experts often can't reliably pick a Stradivarius from a modern violin.

questions.question: Why did people once cool buildings in hot climates without any electricity?

answers.text: Wind towers funnelled breezes and evaporating water cooled the air
Thick walls were packed with blocks of imported ice
Underground fires created a draft that pulled heat out

questions.fun_fact: Persian 'badgirs' caught wind and drew it down over pools or damp surfaces; as the water evaporated it stole heat, chilling the incoming air. The same evaporative-cooling physics runs through modern swamp coolers.

questions.question: Why did salt and sugar preserve food for centuries before refrigeration existed?

answers.text: They pull water out of microbes and dry them to death
They coat the food in an airtight crystal shell
They lower the food's temperature as they dissolve

questions.fun_fact: Heavy salt or sugar makes the surrounding water so concentrated that osmosis sucks moisture out of any bacteria, shrivelling them. That's why salted fish, ham and jam keep for months at room temperature.

questions.question: Why did a compass let medieval sailors find north long before anyone knew what magnetism was?

answers.text: A magnetised needle aligns with Earth's magnetic field
The needle was drawn toward the bright Pole Star
Ocean currents nudged the floating needle northward

questions.fun_fact: Earth behaves like a giant magnet, so a freely pivoting magnetised needle swings to point roughly north. Chinese navigators used floating lodestone compasses centuries before Europeans, with no theory of why it worked.

questions.question: Why did ancient Roman roads survive two thousand years of traffic and weather?

answers.text: Layered stone and gravel let water drain and spread loads
The stones were fused together with molten iron
They were carved from single giant slabs of bedrock

questions.fun_fact: Roman engineers built up multiple layers — a deep rubble base, gravel, then tight-fitting paving stones — and crowned the surface so rainwater ran off into side ditches. Keeping water out of the foundation is exactly why they lasted.

questions.question: Why did medieval stained glass makers add gold to get a deep red colour?

answers.text: Tiny gold particles scatter light to appear ruby red
Gold was the only pigment that survived the furnace
Gold reflected sunlight to brighten the whole window

questions.fun_fact: 'Ruby gold' glass owes its colour to gold nanoparticles suspended in the melt, which scatter light toward red — an accidental brush with nanotechnology centuries early. The same effect colours the famous Roman Lycurgus Cup, which glows green or red depending on the light.

questions.question: Why did early submarine crews have to surface so often before modern air systems?

answers.text: Exhaled carbon dioxide built up and poisoned the air
The hull leaked too much to stay down for long
Cold deep water froze the engines solid

questions.fun_fact: Running out of oxygen is rarely the first danger in a sealed space — rising CO2 is. It makes crews drowsy and breathless long before the oxygen is gone, which is why early subs surfaced frequently to vent and refresh the air.

questions.question: Why was the modern necktie originally worn, according to its name's French origin?

answers.text: It copied scarves worn by Croatian soldiers
It marked a sailor's rank at sea
It held a nobleman's collar shut in cold weather

questions.fun_fact: The French word 'cravate' came from 'Croate' (Croatian) after 17th-century Croatian mercenaries in Paris wore knotted neck scarves that Parisians copied as fashion.

questions.question: Why are dishes served with spinach often called 'Florentine'?

answers.text: A French queen from Florence adored spinach
Spinach was first farmed near Florence
A Florentine painter only ate green food

questions.fun_fact: Catherine de' Medici left Florence to marry into French royalty and supposedly demanded spinach at every meal, so French cooks tagged spinach dishes 'à la florentine' in her honour.

questions.question: The word 'salary' aside, which common word comes from the Roman day when monthly debts fell due?

answers.text: 'Candidate', from the white togas of office-seekers
'Calendar' itself, from 'calends', the day debts were called
'Census', from counting heads at festivals

questions.fun_fact: 'Calendar' comes from the Latin 'kalendae', the first day of each month when debts fell due and account books — the 'calendarium' — were settled.

questions.question: Why do we call unwanted bulk email 'spam'?

answers.text: From a Monty Python sketch repeating a tinned-meat brand
It's an acronym for 'sales promotion and marketing'
Named after a programmer called Sam P. Ackerman

questions.fun_fact: In a 1970 Monty Python's Flying Circus sketch a café menu drowns in repetitions of 'Spam', so early internet users adopted the word for messages that crowd out everything else.

questions.question: What is the real reason ketchup was originally bottled and sold?

answers.text: As a medicine sold in pill form
As a wood stain for furniture
As a fuel additive for lamps

questions.fun_fact: In the 1830s an American doctor branded tomato ketchup as a cure for indigestion and even sold it as concentrated 'tomato pills' before it became a condiment.

questions.question: According to popular legend, why is the breakfast pastry called a 'croissant' shaped like a crescent?

answers.text: To celebrate a victory over Ottoman forces
To fit neatly around a coffee cup
To copy the shape of a baker's oven door

questions.fun_fact: Legend ties the crescent shape to bakers mocking the Ottoman crescent emblem after the 1683 Siege of Vienna, though the buttery French croissant we know was perfected much later in Paris and its true origin is uncertain.

questions.question: What was the original purpose of the small 'fifth pocket' inside the right front pocket of jeans?

answers.text: To hold a pocket watch
To store spare rivets
To carry matches kept dry

questions.fun_fact: Levi's added the tiny pocket in the 1870s specifically so working men could tuck away a pocket watch; it long outlived the gadget it was designed for.

questions.question: Why does the word 'quarantine' specifically suggest a period of forty?

answers.text: Ships were isolated for forty days during plague
Forty was the Roman legal limit for any detention
Doctors believed illness peaked on the fortieth hour

questions.fun_fact: Venetian authorities made arriving ships wait 'quaranta giorni' — forty days — before docking during plague outbreaks, and the Italian for forty gave us the word.

questions.question: Why is the radio distress call 'Mayday' that particular word?

answers.text: From the French 'm'aidez', meaning 'help me'
Named after a ship that sank in May
From a captain named Matthew Day

questions.fun_fact: A London radio officer coined it in 1923 from the French 'venez m'aider' ('come help me') because much air traffic at the time was between England and France.

questions.question: What accidental discovery led to the invention of the microwave oven?

answers.text: A chocolate bar melted in an engineer's pocket
A radar dish overheated a cup of tea
A lightning strike cooked a stored chicken

questions.fun_fact: Engineer Percy Spencer noticed a chocolate bar melting near an active radar magnetron in 1945; he then deliberately popped corn and exploded an egg to confirm the cooking effect.

questions.question: Why do British police carry the nickname 'bobbies'?

answers.text: After the politician who founded the force, Robert Peel
From the bobbing helmets they once wore
After a famous first constable named Bob

questions.fun_fact: Robert Peel set up London's Metropolitan Police in 1829, so officers were nicknamed 'bobbies' (and earlier 'peelers') after his first name and surname.

questions.question: What was the original, non-musical purpose of the saxophone's inventor in creating it?

answers.text: To bridge the gap between brass and woodwind in military bands
To amplify foghorns for harbour ships
To test the acoustics of opera houses

questions.fun_fact: Adolphe Sax patented the saxophone in the 1840s aiming to give marching military bands an instrument that carried outdoors better than strings yet blended brass power with woodwind agility.

questions.question: Why is a sandwich called a 'sandwich'?

answers.text: After an earl who wanted to eat without leaving his card table
After a beach town where it was first sold
From an old word meaning 'pressed bread'

questions.fun_fact: The 4th Earl of Sandwich reputedly asked for meat between bread so he could keep gambling one-handed, and companions began ordering 'the same as Sandwich'.

questions.question: What was the Slinky originally being developed to do?

answers.text: Stabilise sensitive instruments on rocking ships
Measure earthquakes in remote valleys
Untangle telephone wires automatically

questions.fun_fact: Naval engineer Richard James was experimenting with tension springs to keep shipboard equipment steady in 1943 when one tumbled off a shelf and 'walked' — inspiring the toy.

questions.question: Why does the word 'cappuccino' refer to a coffee drink?

answers.text: Its colour resembled the brown robes of Capuchin friars
It was first brewed in a town called Cappucci
It was named after a barista, Carlo Cappuccini

questions.fun_fact: The drink's light brown shade matched the hooded habits of Capuchin monks, whose order also lent its name to the capuchin monkey for the same reason.

questions.question: What was unusual about the route of the 1908 'New York to Paris' automobile race?

answers.text: It was driven mostly westward across three continents
It used only electric cars the whole way
It was completed entirely without refuelling

questions.fun_fact: Competitors drove west from New York across the United States, were shipped to Asia, then crossed Siberia and Europe to Paris — a roughly 22,000-mile route that took the winner 169 days.

questions.question: Why are the wide leather chairs in barbershops historically tied to surgery?

answers.text: Barbers once performed bloodletting and minor surgery
Surgeons borrowed barbers' chairs for operations
Barbershops doubled as recovery wards

questions.fun_fact: For centuries 'barber-surgeons' cut hair and also pulled teeth, set bones and let blood; the red-and-white barber pole represents blood and the bandages used to wrap the arm.

questions.question: What is the real origin of the phrase 'the whole nine yards'?

answers.text: It remains genuinely unknown despite many claims
It refers to a standard bolt of cloth for a kilt
It refers to fighter-plane machine-gun belts

questions.fun_fact: Etymologists have hunted for decades, and the popular ammunition-belt and tailoring stories are unproven; the earliest printed uses don't even agree on the number, making this a celebrated unsolved origin.

questions.question: Why is a marathon race that particular distance, tied to ancient Greece?

answers.text: After a messenger's run from the town of Marathon
It was the length of an Olympic stadium track times forty
It matched the daily march of a Spartan army

questions.fun_fact: The race honours the legend of a runner carrying news of victory from Marathon to Athens; the modern 42.195 km distance traces to the 1908 London Olympics and was officially standardised in 1921.

questions.question: What was the surprising original use of bubble wrap when it was invented in 1957?

answers.text: Textured wallpaper for homes
Insulation for greenhouse roofs
Padding for athletic shoes

questions.fun_fact: Two engineers sealed two shower curtains together hoping to sell trendy three-dimensional wallpaper; it flopped, and only later did they pitch the air pockets as protective packaging.

questions.question: Why does the word 'denim', the fabric of jeans, point to a French city?

answers.text: It comes from 'de Nîmes', meaning 'from Nîmes'
It was named after a tailor, Henri Denim
It comes from the French word for 'durable'

questions.fun_fact: The sturdy twill was 'serge de Nîmes' — serge from the town of Nîmes — while 'jeans' separately comes from Genoa, the Italian port whose sailors wore the cotton cloth.

questions.question: What was Coca-Cola's rival 7 Up originally marketed as containing?

answers.text: A mood-stabilising drug, lithium
Crushed citrus seeds for vitamins
Trace amounts of real gold flakes

questions.fun_fact: Launched in 1929 as 'Bib-Label Lithiated Lemon-Lime Soda', it contained lithium citrate, a compound later used to treat mood disorders; the lithium was removed in 1948.

questions.question: Why do we say a clumsy mistake is a 'blooper', a word born in early broadcasting?

answers.text: From the 'bloop' sound of a recording error
After a comedian named Sid Blooper
From a Dutch word for 'red face'

questions.fun_fact: Early radio and TV engineers called the low 'bloop' noise made when a sound recording was cut or spliced wrong a 'blooper', and the term spread to mean any on-air flub.

questions.question: What was the original purpose of high-heeled shoes, centuries before fashion?

answers.text: To help cavalry riders grip their stirrups
To keep feet above flooded city streets
To make soldiers appear taller in formation

questions.fun_fact: Persian horsemen wore heeled riding boots so their feet locked into stirrups while shooting bows; European aristocrats later adopted heels as a manly status symbol before women's fashion claimed them.

questions.question: Roughly how long ago did the last woolly mammoths still walk the Earth?

answers.text: They were still alive when the Egyptian pyramids stood
They died out a million years before any human civilisation
They vanished just as the dinosaurs disappeared

questions.fun_fact: A small population survived on Wrangel Island off Siberia until around 2000 BC. The Great Pyramid of Giza was already about 500 years old by the time the very last mammoths died.

questions.question: How many years separate Cleopatra from the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza?

answers.text: About 2,500 years
About 500 years
About 5,000 years

questions.fun_fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the pyramids. The pyramids were already ancient tourist attractions when she was queen.

questions.question: Who made the first powered flight with this machine in 1903?

answers.text: Otto Lilienthal
The Wright brothers
Louis Blériot

questions.fun_fact: The first flight on 17 December 1903 lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — less than the wingspan of a modern Boeing 747. The fourth attempt that same day managed 260 metres.

questions.question: Which crisis does this famous 1936 photograph belong to?

answers.text: The Great Depression
The First World War
The oil crisis

questions.fun_fact: Dorothea Lange photographed Florence Owens Thompson at a pea-pickers' camp in California — six exposures in ten minutes. The government sent food to the camp afterwards; the family had already moved on.

questions.question: Which US president is shown here?

answers.text: Ulysses S. Grant
Andrew Jackson
Abraham Lincoln

questions.fun_fact: Alexander Gardner took this portrait in November 1863, days before the Gettysburg Address. Lincoln was the first US president photography followed closely — over 130 pictures of him survive.

questions.question: Which ship is leaving Southampton here on 10 April 1912?

answers.text: The Lusitania
The Titanic
The Britannic

questions.fun_fact: Five days later she was on the sea floor. Only three of the four funnels were real — the rear one served ventilation, and the impression that four funnels made.

questions.question: Which 1989 event brought this crowd to the Brandenburg Gate?

answers.text: The uprising of 17 June 1953
The Berlin Blockade
The fall of the Berlin Wall

questions.fun_fact: The wall opened on 9 November 1989, but the Brandenburg Gate itself only on 22 December — for six weeks the city's best-known landmark still stood in the restricted zone while the celebrating went on beside it.
